scribe_response.text: Tell me about your first job. My first real job was in a dressmaker's, dressmaker's shop called Madame Lim's, in Iloilo. I was sixteen, and I worked there on Saturdays to help pay for my books. The shop was a long narrow room, hot as an uh oven, with ten sewing machines. Madame Lim was not really a madame, um but she liked the title because it sounded elegant. She was a tiny woman with um a measuring tape draped around her neck like um a scarf. She wore thick glasses, and she could spot a crooked seam from across the room. My first task was to sort buttons, with a huge biscuit tin in my lap. There were thousands of them, in brass and mother of pearl and every color of plastic. I thought it was the most boring work in the world. But Madame Lim said a person who cannot sort buttons cannot be trusted with scissors. After three weeks she let me sew hems, and I felt promoted to queen. The fabrics were wonderful, with pink satin for weddings and crisp cotton for school uniforms. I loved the smell of new cloth and the soft sound of the shears. My fingers were pricked a hundred times, and I learned to suck away the blood. What happened next? Madame Lim paid me fifteen pesos a week, which seemed like um a fortune. I gave ten to my mother and kept five, and with it I bought uh a small mirror. My coworkers were four older women who gossiped from morning to night and fed me sweet bread. Aling Pacita sang old love songs and cried a little at every high uh note. Young Remedios was getting married, and we all stitched her wedding gown together. It took two months, and I sewed three hundred tiny pearl, pearl beads along the neckline. On the wedding day I peeked into the church and saw the uh dress glowing. I felt a deep, private pride, because my stitches um were holding that bride together. That job taught me patience, because you, you cannot rush a seam or hide a mistake. It also taught me about people, because customers told their whole lives while being measured. I learned that a woman standing in her slip will say anything. Madame Lim taught me to look closely and to be honest, even when the cloth was expensive. She said a good dress is a kindness, because it helps a person feel brave. One afternoon a rich lady complained that her blouse was too tight. Can you tell me more about that? Madame Lim calmly let out the seam and told her the blouse had been perfect. I learned that sometimes uh diplomacy is a form of tailoring. During the typhoon season the roof leaked, and we covered the fabric with plastic sheets. I worked there for two years, until I went to teachers college. On my um last day Madame Lim gave me silver scissors wrapped in a handkerchief. She said a, a teacher also cuts and sews, only with words and children. I still have those um scissors, and they sit in my sewing box in Abu Dhabi. Every time I make a dress for my granddaughter, I think of that hot little room. My fingers still remember how to hold a needle without looking. Not every first job is glamorous, but a good one teaches you how to begin. I sometimes tell my students that even sorting buttons can be the start of something great. They usually laugh, um but I mean every word. That tiny shop um made me patient, careful, and proud of ordinary work. I would walk back into it um tomorrow, with a biscuit tin in my lap.
